title: The Senior Examiner's Full Mark Story Opening
author: Salles, Mr
summary: This piece decodes a published 'full mark' exemplar creative-writing story from a GCSE senior examiner, arguing that the actual skill being tested is not literary quality but pattern-matching to what a specific examiner's mark scheme rewards: description even where the official criteria no longer require it, particular forms of repetition used as sentence-variation devices, physical sensations used to convey emotion, and carefully controlled punctuation choices like avoiding exclamation marks (associated with 'immature' writing). The author explicitly separates personal literary judgment (he finds the exemplar's style overwrought and finds it funny) from strategic advice, arguing students should 'steal' the sentence types, structural moves, and clichés on display, since ideas themselves cannot be plagiarized, and reframes the whole exercise as playing a specific, learnable game rather than producing original literature. The piece then breaks the exemplar down using the hero's-journey story structure (introduction, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution), explicitly presenting it as a reusable template that can be adapted to any exam prompt regardless of the specific question asked, positioning genre-savvy technique over inspiration as the reliable path to a top grade.
points: The core reframe: the examiner 'doesn't know what good writing is, they simply know the mark scheme and what they like' — success means matching the examiner's specific preferences, not producing objectively strong literature.
Even techniques removed from the official mark scheme (like descriptive writing) are shown to still be implicitly expected and rewarded by the actual examiner in practice.

Specific transferable techniques are named: physical-sensation descriptions of emotion, deliberate short sentences and fragments, favored repetition patterns, and avoiding exclamation marks as a marker of 'immature' writing.

The hero's-journey structure is broken into five explicit stages (introduction/exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution) and presented as a reusable template adaptable to any exam prompt regardless of the specific question.

The piece explicitly frames this as legitimate strategy rather than plagiarism, since 'ideas are free' — students can steal sentence types, structural moves, and clichés from the exemplar as long as they change the specific wording.
quotes: The examiner doesn't know what good writing is, they simply know the mark scheme and what they like. Give them what they like!
You realise that, even though descriptive techniques are no longer part of the mark scheme, the examiner 100% expects to see description. Give it to them.
Ideas are free - you can steal every single idea in this story, without plagiarism.
The hero's quest is a classic story structure, and you can fit it to any question.
You can easily change the characters and setting, but follow exactly the same journey for your story. It will fit every single question.
That's the way the examiner thinks. Not, 'is this good writing?' but 'does this hit all the bullet points in the mark scheme?' So, you learn to play the game - give the examiner what they want.
